sec.p: Congenital malformations of the inner ear, such as Mondini malformation, common cavity malformation, and various cochlear or vestibular developmental abnormalities, are significant causes of severe or profound hearing loss (101). These lesions not only help clarify the origin of the hearing loss but may also indicate clinical risks, including cerebrospinal fluid leaks, recurrent meningitis, or increased complexity during surgical interventions. Thus, imaging assessment in these pediatric patients is not merely an anatomical adjunct; it is essential for establishing therapeutic strategies. Molecular testing can further validate imaging results in children with EVA or other imaging abnormalities, enhancing the accuracy of etiological classification.

Cochlear nerve deficiency (CND) is a primary focus for imaging evaluation in cases of unilateral and bilateral severe hearing loss. MRI is particularly adept at detecting hypoplasia, agenesis, and associated anomalies of the brainstem auditory circuits (102). The clinical significance of these findings lies in their direct implications for future auditory implant strategies. In individuals with significant structural anomalies of the cochlear nerve, the effectiveness of conventional CI may be limited. Some pediatric patients may require further evaluation for alternative interventions, such as auditory brainstem implantation (ABI). Conversely, for children primarily experiencing conductive or mixed hearing loss alongside specific anatomical anomalies, tailored reconstructive approaches—such as bone-conduction implants—might prove more appropriate (103).

The role of imaging assessments in managing perinatal and NICU-related hearing concerns extends beyond merely enhancing anatomical understanding; it also facilitates the transition from phenotypic characterization of hearing loss to etiological identification. Imaging studies should be a core component of the assessment framework for high-risk children, particularly those with severe or unilateral hearing loss, suspected genetic disorders, or those being considered for cochlear implants. Integrating this information with audiology, genetic testing, and clinical exposure history is crucial. Clear localization of the etiology enables more targeted auditory rehabilitation decisions and long-term prognosis assessments.

Perinatal and NICU-related hearing concerns arise not from a singular event, but from a confluence of various biological and iatrogenic exposures, compounded by developmental immaturity. Prematurity, hypoxia, illness, hyperbilirubinemia, ototoxic medicines, and the degree of circulatory support collectively influence the range of auditory susceptibility in high-risk newborns. For this population, complete screening before discharge is simply the initial step in risk identification. The essential factor is the implementation of a continuous, stratified, and multimodal follow-up system based on exposure intensity and etiological indicators, aimed at early identification and intervention of auditory function abnormalities prior to critical periods for language and neurological development.

sec.title: Clinical implications: from etiological recognition to risk-informed surveillance
Interpreting risk indicators beyond the newborn screen
sec.p: The evidence reviewed above indicates that pediatric hearing loss should not be conceptualized solely as a condition either detected or excluded at birth. UNHS remains indispensable for the early identification of congenital hearing loss. However, it remains a cross-sectional assessment performed at a single developmental time point. Its performance is limited for conditions that emerge after the neonatal period, progress gradually, fluctuate over time, or primarily affect neural synchrony rather than cochlear outer hair cell function (6, 104). This limitation is particularly relevant for children with cCMV infection, pathogenic or likely pathogenic deafness-related variants, a positive family history, NICU exposure, or syndromic features (105–107).

A central implication is that risk indicators should be interpreted as signals of future auditory vulnerability rather than as established hearing loss (108). Some indicators, such as confirmed congenital infection or biallelic pathogenic variants in well-characterized genes, may provide relatively direct etiological information. Others, including prematurity, low birth weight, hypoxia, hyperbilirubinemia, sepsis, or exposure to ototoxic medication, often function as components of a broader vulnerability profile. Their significance lies not only in their individual associations with hearing loss but also in their potential to interact with developmental immaturity, genetic susceptibility, and postnatal exposures.

This distinction is important because it helps to eliminate two common interpretive errors: false reassurance after a normal newborn screen and overmedicalization of infants who carry risk markers but have no current audiological abnormality (108). A balanced approach requires clinicians and researchers to distinguish confirmed disease, probable etiology, susceptibility, and contextual risk. In this framework, the value of risk indicators is not to replace audiological diagnosis, but to identify children for whom a single normal screening result may be insufficient.

sec.title: Linking etiology, phenotype, and audiological assessment
sec.p: Etiological information is most useful when interpreted alongside clinical phenotype and age-appropriate audiological assessment. Genetic forms of hearing loss illustrate this principle clearly. GJB2-related hearing loss may span from congenital severe impairment to mild, delayed-onset, or progressive phenotypes; SLC26A4-related disease is frequently associated with enlarged vestibular aqueduct and fluctuating or progressive hearing loss; OTOF-related disease may present as ANSD with preserved OAE but abnormal ABR; and mt-RNR1 variants primarily indicate susceptibility to aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity (109, 110). These examples illustrate that genetic findings should not be interpreted as uniform predictors of severity, but as context-dependent markers that require phenotypic correlation.

Infectious etiologies also necessitate longitudinal interpretation. cCMV is particularly significant as many affected infants are asymptomatic at birth and may pass newborn hearing screenings while remaining at risk for delayed-onset, progressive, or fluctuating SNHL (106). Unlike stable congenital hearing loss, cCMV-related auditory impairment may evolve non-linearly, vary between ears, and interact with broader neurodevelopmental outcomes. Thus, the clinical significance of cCMV rests not only in its role as an etiological diagnosis but also in its capacity to identify children whose auditory trajectory may remain uncertain following the neonatal period.

Perinatal and NICU-related exposures further illustrate the necessity of linking risk indicators with lesion-level phenotypes. Severe hyperbilirubinemia, hypoxia, infection, mechanical ventilation, and ototoxic drug exposure can impact the cochlea, auditory nerve, brainstem auditory pathways, or central auditory networks (107, 111). Some children may exhibit threshold elevation, while others may demonstrate neural conduction abnormalities or disproportionate difficulties in speech perception. Consequently, relying on a single test modality may prove inadequate for certain high-risk groups. OAE, ABR, immittance measures, ASSR, behavioral audiometry, and speech perception testing each provide distinct information, with their relevance varying by age, suspected lesion level, and developmental stage (112–114).

sec.title: Implications for risk-based follow-up
sec.p: The findings summarized in this review advocate for a risk-based approach to post-screening surveillance, with careful definition of its purpose (104, 106–108). This approach should not be interpreted as a universal mandate for intensive follow-up for all infants or as a rigid management algorithm. Instead, it should be recognized as a principle aimed at aligning the intensity of surveillance with the strength, specificity, and persistence of risk indicators. Children with confirmed etiological diagnoses, such as cCMV, well-characterized pathogenic variants, or syndromic features, may necessitate closer developmental observation compared to those with isolated, weak, or transient risk markers (106).

Risk-based follow-up must also account for developmental timing. Delayed-onset and progressive hearing loss can manifest clinically during infancy, toddlerhood, preschool years, or even later in childhood (108). These critical periods coincide with rapid language development, social communication, and early learning. Consequently, surveillance strategies should not only consider auditory thresholds but also incorporate parental concerns, speech-language milestones, listening behaviors, and functional communication. In cases of suspected ANSD, unilateral hearing loss, or central auditory involvement, speech perception and real-world listening challenges may provide more insightful information than pure-tone thresholds alone (112–114).

Risk-based surveillance at the level of public health should be feasible, proportionate, and fair (115, 116). Systems that identify more at-risk infants without confirming a diagnosis will increase the demand for healthcare services due to poor communication with parents and a failure to intervene. Failure to consider the risk index may lead to the progression of undetected, slow-onset hearing loss and thus miss the window for intervention. Based on the above review, not all children need to be screened frequently; rather, according to their reasons for needing screening and any other risk factors, some children may require more often.

sec.title: Evidence gaps and future directions
Clarifying causality and risk magnitude
sec.p: Although many etiologies and risk indicators for pediatric hearing loss have been identified, the strength of evidence varies substantially across domains. Genetic causes, cCMV, severe hyperbilirubinemia, ototoxic exposure, and structural inner ear abnormalities have relatively clear mechanistic or clinical links to childhood hearing loss (111). In contrast, evidence for several prenatal environmental, metabolic, immune, paternal, and epigenetic exposures remains less definitive (87–89). These factors are biologically plausible and may contribute to auditory vulnerability, but their independent effects are difficult to isolate because they often co-occur with socioeconomic disadvantage, maternal illness, prematurity, infection, or healthcare access barriers. Specifically, elevated serum uric acid and aberrant uric acid metabolism may contribute to such metabolic pathways of hearing impairment, potentially through the induction of oxidative stress and microvascular dysfunction in the cochlea. Furthermore, in certain pediatric hereditary or complex disorders, aberrant uric acid metabolism frequently co-occurs with auditory dysfunction.

Future studies should move beyond simple exposure–outcome associations and clarify causal pathways, dose–response relationships, timing of vulnerability, and interactions among multiple risks. Prospective birth cohorts with repeated audiological assessment, standardized exposure measurement, genomic or molecular data, and developmental follow-up would be particularly valuable. Such designs could help distinguish factors that directly cause hearing loss from those that function primarily as markers of broader developmental risk. This distinction is essential for developing clinically meaningful risk stratification systems.

sec.title: Improving genotype–phenotype and etiology–phenotype correlation
sec.p: A second major gap concerns the relationship between molecular or etiological findings and clinical phenotype. Genetic testing has improved diagnostic yield, but interpretation remains challenging when variants have incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, uncertain pathogenicity, or age-dependent effects (117, 118). The same gene may be associated with different degrees of severity, timing of onset, progression, and treatment response. Similarly, cCMV-related hearing loss may be unilateral or bilateral, stable or fluctuating, congenital or delayed-onset, whereas NICU-related hearing loss may involve cochlear, neural, or central mechanisms (111).

Future research should prioritize longitudinal genotype–phenotype and etiology–phenotype mapping. Studies should report not only whether hearing loss is present, but also its age of onset, laterality, progression, audiometric configuration, speech perception profile, electrophysiological features, imaging findings, and developmental outcomes. This level of phenotypic detail is necessary to identify which children are most likely to benefit from extended surveillance and which markers have limited predictive value. Avoiding both under-recognition of delayed-onset disease and unnecessary medicalization of low-risk children is essential.

sec.title: Evaluating screening expansion, implementation feasibility, and equity
sec.p: Advances in genetic testing and pathogen detection have enhanced interest in combining UNHS with molecular or infectious screening (119–122). Such approaches may improve identification of infants at risk for delayed-onset or progressive hearing loss, particularly in the context of cCMV or pharmacogenetic susceptibility. However, expanded screening raises important questions about cost-effectiveness, informed consent, variant interpretation, parental anxiety, follow-up capacity, and equitable access (123–126). Higher diagnostic yield does not directly translate into better child outcomes if health systems cannot provide timely confirmation, counseling, monitoring, and intervention.

Considering this, future evaluations should assess screening strategies using established implementation and outcome indicators rather than a separate public health assessment matrix. Relevant indicators may include screening coverage, referral completion, diagnostic confirmation, loss to follow-up or loss to documentation, age at diagnosis, age at intervention, access to audiological and rehabilitation services, family understanding of results, cost-effectiveness, and disparities by socioeconomic status, geography, ethnicity, language, and healthcare access (125, 126). This is particularly important in resource-restrained settings, where the most effective strategy may not be the most technologically advanced, but the one that consistently links identification with follow-up and intervention. Equity should be treated as a core dimension of screening effectiveness rather than a secondary implementation concern.

sec.title: Toward developmentally informed surveillance
sec.p: The broader challenge for the field is to develop surveillance models that acknowledge the developmental nature of childhood hearing loss. Many clinically significant forms of hearing impairment do not remain static at birth; they may emerge, progress, fluctuate, or only become functionally apparent when listening demands increase (112–114). Future research should include repeated hearing assessments, speech-language outcomes, caregiver-reported listening behaviors, and neurodevelopmental measures to better reflect the real-world impact of mild, unilateral, neural, or progressive hearing loss.

A developmentally informed research agenda must also integrate data across various disciplines. Fields such as genetics, infectious disease, neonatology, audiology, otolaryngology, speech-language pathology, epidemiology, and public health each offer distinct perspectives (115). The next generation of evidence will require not only improved testing but also better integration of etiological information, clinical phenotype, developmental trajectory, and health system context. Such integration is essential for transitioning from early detection to early recognition of children whose auditory development may remain at risk over time.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The UNHS era has substantially improved the early detection of congenital hearing loss, revealing the complexity of pediatric hearing loss that cannot be fully addressed by a single neonatal screening event. Mild, unilateral, delayed-onset, progressive, and neural forms of hearing loss may escape early detection, and some children who pass newborn screening remain at risk due to genetic susceptibility, congenital infection, intrauterine exposures, NICU-related complications, or syndromic conditions. This review highlights the need to distinguish among etiological causes, risk indicators, and clinical phenotypes. Genetic variants, cCMV, structural inner ear abnormalities, ototoxic susceptibility, and NICU-related exposures differ in mechanism, predictive value, and clinical implications. Likewise, audiological phenotypes vary according to onset timing, lesion level, progression, laterality, and functional impact. Recognizing these distinctions is critical for interpreting risk following UNHS and for identifying children whose hearing and communication development may warrant closer observation. The central implication is that childhood hearing loss should be viewed as a developmental condition characterized by heterogeneous causes and trajectories, rather than as a fixed diagnosis established solely at birth. Together, etiological knowledge, risk indicators, and age-appropriate audiological assessments provide a stronger foundation for recognizing delayed-onset and progressive hearing loss. Future research should refine risk estimates, clarify causal pathways, enhance genotype–phenotype correlations, and evaluate equitable approaches to post-screening surveillance. By aligning etiological understanding with developmental follow-up, pediatric hearing health systems may decrease missed or delayed diagnoses and improve long-term language, educational, and psychosocial outcomes.
